chapter_title: NoSQL Databases: Key-Value Stores and Document Databases

screens.title: NoSQL Databases: Key-Value Stores & Document Databases
screens.subtitle: When schema flexibility and availability matter more than strict ACID guarantees

narration.text: In this chapter we'll build a clear, practical mental model of why NoSQL databases exist and where key-value and document databases shine. Start by remembering that relational databases give you strong transactional guarantees and structured schemas, but at scale those advantages can become constraints. NoSQL shifts the balance: it trades immediate consistency for greater availability and schema flexibility, embracing BASE properties and designs optimized for horizontal scale. You'll learn the CAP theorem and how the inevitability of network partitions forces choices between consistency and availability. We'll then look at the simplest NoSQL type—the key-value store—where keys map to opaque values and reads and writes are extremely fast, with Redis and DynamoDB as representative examples. After that, we'll step up to document databases like MongoDB, which store semi-structured JSON documents, support rich queries on internal fields, and encourage denormalized models for faster reads. Along the way you'll see concrete code examples, common modeling mistakes, and a hands-on activity that has you design user preference storage in both models. By the end, you should be able to choose the appropriate NoSQL model for a given set of availability, consistency, and data-shape requirements, and explain the practical trade-offs to an interviewer or teammate.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: NoSQL offers alternative data models that prioritize availability and flexible schemas; choose the model by matching data shape and read/write patterns to CAP trade-offs.

narration.text: By the end of these screens you will have four concrete, verifiable skills. First, you'll be able to contrast S Q L and NoSQL, not just by vocabulary, but by the consequences for schema evolution and scaling strategies. You will explain why rigid schemas and ACID transactions can be limiting for high-volume, evolving workloads. Second, you will understand the CAP theorem and what it forces designers to choose when a network partition happens; you'll be able to explain real trade-offs between consistency and availability with concrete examples. Third, you will identify when a key-value store like Redis or DynamoDB is the right tool: low-latency lookups, caching, and single-object stores where internal value structure is not queried. screens.title: Why NoSQL — when relational databases are limited
screens.subtitle: Schema rigidity, vertical scaling limits, and evolving data requirements

narration.text: Relational databases are built around structured tables, fixed schemas, and strong transactional guarantees. That makes them excellent for bookkeeping, financial systems, and workloads where consistency across multiple records matters. But as systems scale and requirements change, that rigid schema becomes costly to evolve and vertical scaling hits practical limits. NoSQL is shorthand for a set of alternative data models that relax some relational assumptions to favor scale and flexibility. A clear way to define NoSQL is: a family of databases that optimize for particular data shapes and operational goals rather than a single universal model. For example, a social feed with many varied metadata fields and high write and read throughput benefits from flexible documents or key-value lookups rather than repeatedly altering a table schema. A concrete example: adding new optional profile fields in a large user table requires schema migrations in S Q L, while a document store accepts the new keys without changing other documents. A common misconception is that NoSQL means "no consistency"; the right interpretation is that many NoSQL systems prefer eventual consistency to remain available under partition. The takeaway: NoSQL offers targeted solutions for scale and evolving schemas, and your choice must match the application's read/write patterns and tolerance for stale data.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: NoSQL is a family of databases optimized for scale and flexible data shapes, trading some ACID guarantees when appropriate.

content.html:
Core Concept

Why NoSQL

When schema evolution and horizontal scale matter more than strict ACID constraints.

Key points
  • NoSQL supports multiple data models tuned to different patterns.
  • Schema flexibility reduces migration cost as fields evolve.
  • Systems often accept eventual consistency to gain availability and partition tolerance.
Concrete example
A user profile service needs to add optional social links and preferences rapidly. With a document store you can add keys per document without a schema migration; with SQL you must alter the table or use a separate keyed table.
Common mistake
Assuming NoSQL always sacrifices consistency entirely. Many NoSQL systems allow tunable consistency or transactions for subsets of operations.
Key Takeaway

Choose NoSQL when flexible schema and horizontal scalability align with your application's read/write patterns and consistency tolerance.

Definition panel
NoSQL is shorthand for multiple non-relational database types — key-value, document, column-family, and graph — each tuned for specific data shapes and operational trade-offs. They generally replace rigid schemas and favor horizontal scalability.
Metaphor
Think of SQL as a rigid filing cabinet where each drawer has labelled folders, and NoSQL as a set of flexible binders you can add pages to without reformatting everything.
Why it matters
Easier schema changes speed feature iteration and horizontal scaling reduces single-node bottlenecks for high-throughput systems.

screens.title: ACID vs BASE
screens.subtitle: How NoSQL's BASE properties contrast with ACID transactional guarantees

narration.text: ACID and BASE describe two different approaches to correctness and availability in data systems. ACID—Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability—ensures that multi-step operations behave like single atomic actions and that data remains correct across concurrent operations. This is essential for domains like financial transactions. BASE—Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent—captures the trade-offs many NoSQL systems accept to gain availability and partition tolerance. Basically Available means the system will try to respond to every request; Soft state means replicas might differ temporarily; Eventually consistent means replicas converge over time. A practical example: an e-commerce catalog update in a BASE system might show a slightly older price in some regions for a few seconds after an update, whereas ACID systems would block until all replicas confirm the update. A common misconception is that BASE equals “no correctness rules”; instead, BASE systems often provide mechanisms to tune consistency per operation or use compensating actions. The takeaway: match ACID or BASE to your domain’s correctness requirements and latency tolerance, and be prepared to justify where you accept eventual consistency. ACID vs BASE means acid enforces strong correctness; base prioritizes availability and eventual convergence—choose based on domain needs.. In practical terms, how nosql's base properties contrast with acid transactional guarantees. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Contrast
keyIdea.text: ACID enforces strong correctness; BASE prioritizes availability and eventual convergence—choose based on domain needs.

content.html:
Comparison

ACID vs BASE

How transactional guarantees trade off against availability and scale.

ACID (Relational)
  • Strong transactional guarantees across operations.
  • Good for money transfers, inventory reservations, and consistency-critical updates.
  • Tends toward vertical scaling and schema migrations.
Example
A bank transfer must atomically debit one account and credit another, and the system must never see inconsistent balances.
BASE (NoSQL)
  • Prioritizes availability and partition tolerance; accepts eventual consistency.
  • Enables horizontal scaling and flexible schemas.
  • Often used for caching, sessions, and rapidly evolving document data.
Example
A social feed can show slightly stale content to users; availability is preferred over blocking requests during partial failures.
Misconception check
BASE does not mean data is unreliable. It means the system provides different guarantees and often provides ways to tune consistency per operation or to run compensating updates.
Key Takeaway
Pick ACID for correctness-critical domains and BASE for latency and availability at scale, and document the expected inconsistency window.

screens.title: CAP Theorem
screens.subtitle: Why you cannot have Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance together

narration.text: The CAP theorem is a compact lens for thinking about distributed data stores. It states that a distributed system can provide at most two of these three guarantees: Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance. Partition tolerance is generally a given because networks will fail in production; therefore designers must often choose between consistency and availability when a partition happens. Consistency here means that reads always return the most recent write. Availability means every request receives a response, even if that response might be outdated. Consider a geographically replicated key-value store: during a network split, choosing consistency means rejecting writes or reads on some partitions until the cluster can agree—this preserves correctness but reduces availability. Choosing availability means accepting reads and writes on both sides and resolving divergence later, yielding eventual consistency. A frequent misconception is that CAP forces a binary choice system-wide; in practice you can tune consistency per request or use hybrid designs that provide CP behavior for some operations and AP behavior for others. The practical takeaway is to identify the operations in your application that must be strictly consistent and design for CP there, while allowing AP semantics for non-critical or highly available functions.

keyIdea.title: CAP insight
keyIdea.text: Network partitions force a choice between consistency and availability; align that choice with your application's critical operations.

content.html:
Process Flow

CAP Theorem

Understand the forced trade-off and how to map it to application needs.

Consistency (C)
All nodes see the same data at the same time; reads reflect latest writes.
Availability (A)
Every request receives a response, even if it's not the latest state.
Partition tolerance (P)
The system continues to operate despite message loss or node failure.
Concrete scenario
When a network split isolates two replica sets, a CP system will stop serving some operations until consistency is restored; an AP system will continue serving writes and reconcile later.
Practical pattern
Use hybrid designs: treat money transfers as CP, and feed generation or analytics as AP, documenting the acceptable inconsistency windows.
Key Takeaway

Because partitions will happen, design systems by selecting consistency guarantees per operation and by preparing reconciliation mechanisms where you prioritize availability.

narration.text: Key-value stores are the simplest NoSQL model: each record is an association between a unique key and a value. The database treats the value as an opaque blob and does not interpret its internal structure, which makes reads and writes extremely fast and scalable. This model excels when your access patterns are single-key lookups, such as caching session data, user preferences resolved by ID, or feature flags. For instance, using Redis to store session tokens or a user's display name gives you single-digit millisecond reads and simple TTL management. An important practical point is that because the store treats values as opaque, you cannot efficiently query by nested attributes without additional indexing or external systems. A common mistake is trying to use a key-value store for queries like "find all users in city X" when that data is inside JSON values. To summarize, key-value stores are ideal when your primary operations are simple lookups or writes by key, and you accept that more complex queries require different patterns or precomputed indices. Key-Value Stores means key-value stores map unique keys to opaque values; they are ideal for fast lookups and caching but not for rich querying inside values.. In practical terms, simplicity, speed, and opaque values. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Key-value core
keyIdea.text: Key-value stores map unique keys to opaque values; they are ideal for fast lookups and caching but not for rich querying inside values.

content.html:
Definition

Key-Value Stores

A simple mapping from a unique key to an opaque value designed for extreme read/write performance.

When to use
Caching, session storage, user lookups by ID, and configuration storage where queries are by key.
Pitfall
Avoid using key-value stores for attribute-based queries unless you maintain external indices or secondary maps.
Key Takeaway

Use key-value stores for predictable, high-speed single-key operations and caching; plan for additional layers when you need searchability across fields.

Compact example
# Conceptual Redis commands
SET user:123:name "Alice"
SET user:123:theme "dark"
RPUSH user:123:favorite_categories "sports" "news" "tech"
GET user:123:name
Because values are opaque, retrieving users by city or tag requires either additional indices or a document model that exposes those fields to queries.

screens.title: Redis: example commands and a simple Python usage
screens.subtitle: How to set and retrieve keys and store a JSON blob

narration.text: This screen walks through a short Redis usage example to make key-value ideas concrete. The code shows connecting to a Redis instance, setting simple string keys for name and email, and then storing a more complex user profile as a serialized JSON string. The important learning points are practical: using namespaced keys like user:1002:profile helps avoid collisions and makes retrieval straightforward, storing JSON as a string preserves the full object but prevents server-side indexing of its fields, and using TTLs or careful naming can manage cache lifetimes. A common misconception is to think Redis can replace a document database when you need complex queries; Redis excels as an in-memory store and cache but does not natively support querying nested JSON without modules or client-side parsing. After setting keys we retrieve and deserialize the JSON, illustrating the full round trip. The concrete takeaway is to use Redis for extremely low-latency lookups and transient state, and to plan for separate storage or inverted indices when you need searches across object attributes. Redis: example commands and a simple Python usage means use namespaced keys and json serialization for complex objects, but remember values remain opaque to the server unless additional modules are used.. In practical terms, how to set and retrieve keys and store a json blob. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical Redis
keyIdea.text: Use namespaced keys and JSON serialization for complex objects, but remember values remain opaque to the server unless additional modules are used.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

Redis example

Namespaced keys, string values, and storing serialized JSON.

Python example (conceptual)
import redis
import json

# Connect to Redis
r = redis.Redis(host='localhost', port=6379, db=0)

# Set a key-value pair
r.set('user:1001:name', 'Alice Smith')
r.set('user:1001:email', 'alice@example.com')

# Store a more complex object as JSON
user_profile = {
  "id": 1002,
  "name": "Bob Johnson",
  "email": "bob@example.com",
  "last_login": "2023-10-26T10:30:00Z"
}
r.set('user:1002:profile', json.dumps(user_profile))

# Retrieve and deserialize
retrieved = json.loads(r.get('user:1002:profile').decode('utf-8'))
print(retrieved)
What this shows
Use clear key naming conventions and client-side serialization. Redis returns the stored blob; parsing happens on the client. This preserves speed but limits server-side queryability.
When to avoid
If you need to run queries over nested fields or indexes across fields, prefer a document store or maintain auxiliary indices.
Key Takeaway

Redis is excellent for low-latency single-key operations; store structured objects as serialized blobs and plan separate systems for complex search.

screens.title: DynamoDB and distributed key-value scaling
screens.subtitle: Single-digit millisecond performance and horizontal partitioning

narration.text: Amazon DynamoDB is a managed service example often used to illustrate how key-value and document models scale in production. Its core design emphasizes single-digit millisecond latency at any scale by horizontally partitioning data across nodes. The partitioning strategy commonly uses a hash of the primary key to spread traffic. From a design perspective, this means you must select keys thoughtfully to avoid hot partitions and ensure even distribution. One concrete consequence is that read/write capacity planning and key design are part of data modeling. A typical misconception is that managed key-value services automatically solve all scaling problems; they simplify operations, but your access patterns and key choices still determine performance. DynamoDB also supports optional features like secondary indexes and different consistency models for reads, allowing you to tune availability and freshness per operation. The practical takeaway is to think of DynamoDB as a horizontally scalable key-value/document store where operational performance depends on partitioning strategy and the choice of primary keys and indexes. DynamoDB and distributed key-value scaling means managed key-value/document stores scale horizontally; careful key design prevents hot partitions and preserves low latency.. In practical terms, single-digit millisecond performance and horizontal partitioning. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: DynamoDB note
keyIdea.text: Managed key-value/document stores scale horizontally; careful key design prevents hot partitions and preserves low latency.

content.html:
Architecture

DynamoDB & Horizontal Scaling

A managed example showing how key-value/document stores achieve predictable low latency at scale.

Partitioning strategy
Use a hash of the primary key to distribute items. Avoid hot keys that receive disproportionate traffic.
Operational knobs
Provisioned throughput, on-demand scaling, and secondary indexes let you tune latency and query capability.
Consistency options
Choose strongly consistent reads where needed; use eventual consistency for higher read throughput and availability.
Common mistake
Treating the store as fully transparent and ignoring partitioning effects. Key design remains the developer's responsibility.
Key Takeaway

Managed key-value services scale well, but your key and index design control performance and hot-spot risks.

screens.title: Document Databases
screens.subtitle: Semi-structured documents, rich queries, and denormalized models

narration.text: Document databases store semi-structured documents—typically JSON or BSON—where each document is a self-contained unit that can have nested objects and arrays. Documents in the same collection don't need to share an identical schema, which makes the model very flexible for agile development. This flexibility allows embedding related data—like a user's addresses—directly inside a user document so that a single read gives you everything you need, improving read performance for the most common access patterns. A concrete example is storing user profiles with nested name, addresses array, preferences, and tags. Document databases also support rich queries on internal fields and aggregation pipelines for transformation and reporting. A common modeling mistake is to treat the document store like a relational database and overuse references leading to many small reads; conversely, heavy embedding may cause large documents that are expensive to update. The practical guidance is to model by access patterns: embed when you need fast reads of related data together, reference when the related data grows unbounded or is shared widely. That trade-off drives both performance and consistency considerations. Document Databases means document dbs store flexible, nested documents and are best modeled by embedding related data when reads favor a single document fetch.. In practical terms, semi-structured documents, rich queries, and denormalized models. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Document core
keyIdea.text: Document DBs store flexible, nested documents and are best modeled by embedding related data when reads favor a single document fetch.

content.html:
Core Concept

Document Databases

Flexible, nested documents enable rich queries and denormalized reads optimized for common access patterns.

Advantages
Flexible schema, efficient single-document reads, and powerful aggregation tools for analytics and transformation.
Modeling advice
Model by read patterns: embed small, commonly-read related data; reference large or shared entities to avoid oversized documents.
Key Takeaway

Use document databases when your data is naturally hierarchical and you want flexible schemas and efficient reads of nested data.

MongoDB example
// Insert a user document
db.users.insertOne({
  _id: "user1001",
  name: { first: "Alice", last: "Smith" },
  email: "alice@example.com",
  addresses: [
    { type: "home", street: "123 Main St", city: "Anytown", zip: "12345" },
    { type: "work", street: "456 Oak Ave", city: "Otherville", zip: "67890" }
  ],
  preferences: { newsletter: true, theme: "dark" },
  tags: ["premium", "active"]
})

// Query nested field
db.users.find({ "addresses.city": "Anytown" })

narration.text: When modeling with document databases you'll make repeated choices between embedding related data inside a document or referencing it from another collection. Embedding places the related data directly next to the parent, enabling single-document reads that are fast and simple. For example, embedding a user's addresses inside the user document makes it trivial to fetch all addresses with one query. Referencing instead stores a separate document and uses an identifier to point to it; this is useful when the related data grows without bound or is shared across many parents. The trade-offs are clear: embedding improves read performance and reduces the number of queries but increases the cost of updates if the same data is duplicated across many documents. Referencing reduces redundancy but requires additional queries or joins at read time and can be less efficient. A common misconception is to treat embedding as always better; instead, evaluate document size limits, update frequency, and whether the data is shared. The key design heuristic is model for your most common read patterns and accept some redundancy when it meaningfully reduces latency.

keyIdea.title: Modeling trade-off
keyIdea.text: Embed for fast, single-document reads; reference to avoid duplication and manage growing related data.

content.html:
Comparison

Embedding vs Referencing

Balance read performance against redundancy and update cost.

Embed
Fast single-document reads, fewer queries, but can create large documents and duplicate data.
Reference
Keeps documents small and avoids duplication, but requires joins or multiple queries at read time.
Key Takeaway

Model by access: embed when related fields are small and accessed together; reference when they grow large or are widely shared.

Concrete scenario
If orders embed product names to make history immutable and fast to read, updating a product name later requires updating all order documents. If you expect frequent product name changes, use references and resolve names at read time or maintain a denormalized cache with update processes.
Misconception
Denormalization is not a bug; it's a trade-off to improve read latency. Plan update strategies for duplicated fields to avoid inconsistencies.

screens.title: Modeling User Preferences: Key-Value and Document Designs
screens.subtitle: Design patterns and commands for Redis and MongoDB

narration.text: This hands-on activity asks you to model the same user preference data in both a key-value store and a document database. The user data includes theme, notification settings, and favorite categories. For a key-value approach, you would create namespaced keys for each atomic piece of state—SET user:123:theme "dark", SET user:123:notification:email_enabled "true", and use a list or set for favorite categories. Retrieval requires multiple GETs or a small multi-get, which is fine for small preference sets and gives excellent latency. The downside is managing consistency across multiple keys when updating a related set of fields. For a document approach, design a single document like the provided MongoDB example with notification_settings as a nested object and favorite_categories as an array. Updating a single field, like theme, can be done with an update operation targeting that path; querying for all users with push_enabled true uses a query on notification_settings. push_enabled. The trade-offs: documents enable rich queries and single-document atomic updates, while key-value models yield faster per-key access but make multi-field atomicity harder. A common mistake is not thinking through update patterns: if you often update multiple preferences together, prefer the document model. Try both designs mentally and decide which maps to your application's read and write patterns.

keyIdea.title: Activity outcome
keyIdea.text: Modeling the same data in both paradigms clarifies where each excels: single-key speed versus rich queries and atomic document updates.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity

Model user preferences

Design both a key-value layout and a document schema, then weigh pros and cons.

Key-Value (Redis) conceptual commands
# For user_id 123
SET user:123:theme "dark"
SET user:123:notification:email_enabled "true"
SET user:123:notification:push_enabled "true"
SET user:123:notification:sms_enabled "false"
RPUSH user:123:favorite_categories "sports" "news" "tech"
Pros: very fast single-key reads and writes. Cons: multi-field atomic updates require transactions or careful orchestration; querying across fields is difficult.
Document (MongoDB) example
{
  "_id": "user123",
  "theme": "dark",
  "notification_settings": {
    "email_enabled": true,
    "push_enabled": true,
    "sms_enabled": false
  },
  "favorite_categories": ["sports", "news", "tech"]
}

// Update theme only
db.users.updateOne({ _id: 'user123' }, { $set: { theme: 'light' } })

// Query users with push enabled
db.users.find({ "notification_settings.push_enabled": true })
Pros: single-document updates and rich queries. Cons: denormalization can cause redundancy and update complexity when embedded data is duplicated.
Evaluation heuristic
If your app frequently updates multiple preference fields together, prefer the document model. If you need microsecond access to a single field and rarely update groups, key-value is viable.
Key Takeaway
Model by update and query patterns: atomic multi-field updates favor documents; isolated single-key reads favor key-value stores.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's consolidate the essential ideas. NoSQL is not a single technology but a family of databases designed for different data shapes and scaling goals, emphasizing flexibility and availability. BASE summarizes the common properties in many NoSQL systems: basically available, soft state, and eventual consistency, which is a practical alternative to strict ACID guarantees when latency and partition tolerance are primary concerns. The CAP theorem reminds us that during network partitions you must choose between consistency and availability, and practical systems often mix strategies per operation. Key-value stores like Redis and DynamoDB map keys to opaque values and offer unmatched single-key performance, ideal for caching and sessions. Document databases like MongoDB store nested JSON documents that support rich queries and suit hierarchical data. Remember the modeling heuristic: embed when related data is read together and small; reference when it grows large or is shared. With these tools, you can match the datastore to your app's read/write patterns and consistency needs.

keyIdea.title: Essential summary
keyIdea.text: Match data shape and operational needs to the right NoSQL model; use CAP and BASE reasoning to defend your design.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Key Concepts
NoSQL
Not only SQL: a set of models (key-value, document) that prioritize flexibility and scale.
BASE
Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent—an availability-first pattern.
CAP Theorem
A distributed system can choose only two of Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Practical quick-reference for interviews and design reviews

narration.text: Finish by committing these practical heuristics to memory. Key-value stores map keys to opaque values and are great for caching, sessions, and single-key lookups. Document databases hold semi-structured JSON documents, support queries on nested fields, and are ideal when you want flexible schemas and efficient reads of related data. Denormalization—embedding related data—improves read latency but increases duplication and update complexity; reference when data grows or is shared. Finally, always reason about CAP: treat partitions as inevitable and choose consistency guarantees per operation. When answering design questions, state your expected read/write patterns, the acceptable inconsistency window, and the embedding versus referencing rationale. That short checklist will make your datastore choices clear and defensible in an interview or architecture meeting. What to Remember means key-value for single-key speed, document dbs for nested queries, denormalize for reads only when you can manage updates; apply cap to justify trade-offs.. In practical terms, practical quick-reference for interviews and design reviews. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical checklist
keyIdea.text: Key-value for single-key speed, document DBs for nested queries, denormalize for reads only when you can manage updates; apply CAP to justify trade-offs.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Remember
Key-Value
Use for ultra-fast lookups by key and caching; values are opaque unless you add indexing layers.
Document DB
Store nested JSON documents, index internal fields, and design by access patterns for best performance.
Denormalization
Embed for read speed, reference to control growth; always plan update strategies for replicated fields.
Summary Takeaway
When designing, state access patterns, choose a data model that optimizes those patterns, and justify consistency choices with CAP reasoning.
